subject: RFI: Multi-tenant noise floor and quantile decomposition for tail-latency attribution

Subject: RFI: Multi-tenant noise floor and quantile decomposition for tail-latency attribution

Hi Olga,

Thanks for taking this RFI. As part of our evaluation we need detailed methodology and evidence for how Redwood attributes tail-latency to (a) system noise (cloud/transient), (b) multi-tenant interference, (c) caching and batching effects. Specifically, please provide:

- A concise description of the statistical methodology you use to decompose observed latency quantiles into explanatory components (e.g., baseline noise, queuing, kernel variance, tenant interference).
- How you define and measure the "noise floor" and the window(s) used to estimate it.
- Test harness design: how you simulate synthetic tenants, request mixes, and burst profiles; how you control for cross-tenant cache pollution.
- Which metrics you collect (end-to-end latencies, kernel-level histograms, CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit ratios, queuing latency) and sampling cadence.
- Artifacts we can review: representative raw logs, percentile heatmaps, and a short runbook describing experiment controls.

Timeline: we'd like an initial write-up and artifacts by EOD 2026-12-03 and a 30-minute technical call the following week.

Please attach any sample graphs or test plans; we can sign an NDA if needed.

Thanks,
Maria Gomez
Procurement Lead, Artemis Health

Subject: Re: RFI: Multi-tenant noise floor and quantile decomposition for tail-latency attribution

Hi Maria — thanks for the clear list. High level answers and plan below; Ben and Karthik are looped for the deeper artifacts and sample graphs.

Summary (short):
- Methodology: we perform percentile decomposition using paired baseline windows + controlled perturbation experiments. We attribute incremental quantile shifts by running A/B micro-experiments that toggle single variables (batching on/off, cache primed/unprimed, synthetic tenant chatter) while keeping arrival process stationary.
- Noise floor: computed from a cold-window and a stabilized warm-window across 12 separate baseline runs; we report both the median noise and an estimated 95th-percentile noise envelope.
- Test harness: a dedicated, isolated cluster run with synthetic tenants (configurable weight) + a separate witness harness that reports per-tenant kernel-level histograms.

Deliverables we'll attach by 2026-12-03 EOD:
- Redwood multi-tenant test plan (PDF) — outlines experiment matrix and controls.
- Quantile decomposition example graphs (PNG) — p50/p95/p99 overlays for control vs perturbed runs.
- Raw log sample (CSV) — token-level latencies + KV-cache state for one representative run.
- Short runbook (text) — commands we used to prime cache, start tenants, and collect traces.

Next steps: schedule a 30-min technical call — we have availability 2026-12-07 09:00-11:00 PT or 2026-12-08 14:00-16:00 PT. Please confirm which works.

Note: we can provide an NDA for the artifacts if your legal team prefers; otherwise the sample CSV will be scrubbed for PII.

Best,
Olga Petrov
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

To: Maria Gomez <maria.gomez@artemishealth.com>

Date: 2026-12-02T09:15:00Z
Subject: Re: RFI: Multi-tenant noise floor and quantile decomposition for tail-latency attribution

Hi Maria — following up with the technical pattern and a couple of concrete artifacts notes. Below is a compact description of our approach and specific controls to make attribution robust.

Methodology details (engineer friendly):
- Percentile slicing: we compute per-request end-to-end latencies and also annotate each sample with kernel-level tags (scheduling, memcpy, kernel-exec, kvcache-lookup). We then compute conditional percentiles for each tag bucket and use a simple additive decomposition to estimate how much each tag contributes to the incremental shift in p95/p99 between runs.
- Noise floor estimation:
  - Cold-window: 10 independent cold restarts across N=6 nodes to capture variance from JIT/warmup and OS-level scheduling.
  - Warm-window: 30-minute steady traffic window after warmup; we compute rolling 1-min p50/p95/p99 and collapse to a percentile envelope. The noise floor is reported as the 95th percentile of the warm-window p95 across runs.
- Multi-tenant interference fingerprinting:
  - Synthetic tenants: we spin up low, medium, and high noise tenant profiles; each tenant issues a mix of short (interactive) and long (batch) requests using the same model weights. We run pairwise experiments where we keep request rate constant and vary tenant mix.
  - Cache pollution control: use an explicit cache-priming step and a separate unprimed run; track KV cache hit ratio per shard.
- Batching isolation: run experiments (a) batching disabled, (b) batching enabled with fixed batch windows, (c) adaptive batching. We report latency distributions stratified by batch size.

Artifacts and evidence we provide:
- percentile-heatmap.png (stacked heatmap of per-shard p50/p95/p99 across time),
- kernel-latency-breakdown.csv (per-request breakdown),
- synthetic-tenant-config.yaml (fixture),
- runbook.md (commands, environment).

Controlling for cloud transient variability:
- We synchronize clocks and enforce instance pinning (same instance types across runs), perform multiple repeats, and compute bootstrap confidence intervals. We also run a short "no-work" observer process to record background OS/GCE noise. We will include a short section in the runbook that shows how we computed the bootstrap intervals.

Mapping to SLAs: you asked how p95 maps to an SLA. We provide a mapping table where SLA targets map to observed percentiles after accounting for the 95% noise envelope; e.g., to guarantee p95 <= X with 99% confidence we recommend provisioning headroom based on the 95th noise percentile plus the measured incremental p95 delta from tenant interference. We will include a sample table in the PDF.

If useful we can also run a whitebox session where your engineers observe a controlled run remotely.

Cheers,
Ben Carter
Principal Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference

- For the "no-work" observer process, please outline what signals you collect (we want to ensure there is no silent correlation with network ENI throttles in our environment).
- Will the sample CSV include any request payloads? We prefer non-PII; if payloads are necessary, please provide trimmed/hashed values.
